title: Strings and drums
hook: the old kirtan used string instruments and the pakhawaj drum

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghar and rahao, and your line was the house of the tune. Which line in a song kept coming back? Today, the sound itself: what the older kirtan was played on. Day one thousand sixty-four.

A carved wooden body, a skin stretched over its belly, strings running down its neck. In the stories of Guru Nanak's travels, an instrument like that walks the roads beside him: the rabab, in the hands of his companion, Bhai Mardana. In the janamsakhis, the Guru asks Mardana to play, and the hymn comes once the music has begun. So in Sikh memory, kirtan starts with a string being touched. Today: strings and drums.
screen: `WOOD, SKIN, STRINGS.` → `MARDANA'S RABAB.` → `PLAY, AND THE HYMN COMES.`

segments.voice: The phrase is tanti saaj. Saaj is an instrument; tanti, of strings. It's how Sikh musicians name the family of string instruments the older kirtan was played on. The rabab is one. Tradition names others: the saranda, played with a bow; the taus, its body carved like a peacock; the dilruba, a lighter cousin of the taus. Under them sat a drum, the pakhawaj, long and barrel-shaped, played with the hands on both ends. Strings and skin. One carries the melody; the other keeps the beat. Why would that matter to a raga? Because a raga lives partly in the spaces between its notes, the slides and bends that lead from one to the next. A string can slide. A bow can hold a note and lean into it. Today the harmonium and the tabla are a familiar sound in gurdwaras, and they carry much of the kirtan heard there. Alongside them, some musicians and teachers have worked to bring the older strings back, so the ragas can be heard with those slides again. Gurdwaras and kirtan schools make room for both. The Granth itself hears music at the holiest door. In the Japji, in the pauri that asks what the Creator's gate is like, Guru Nanak lists the sounds there: instruments beyond counting, and players beyond counting, all singing. The whole creation is the band. Now look back at the week. The hard century, a kingdom lost and kept, renewal and today, and the year three close. Then raag, why the Granth is sung. Then ghar and rahao. And today the instruments: strings and skin.
screen: `TANTI SAAJ: THE STRING FAMILY.` · `RABAB, SARANDA, TAUS, DILRUBA, PAKHAWAJ.` · `A STRING CAN SLIDE BETWEEN NOTES.` · then, large: `STRINGS AND SKIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for a string instrument. If you can, play a recording of kirtan, or any music with strings in it: a rabab, a sarangi, a violin, a guitar. Close your eyes and follow only the string. Listen for the slide, the place where a key would jump from note to note and a string can glide between them. Then listen underneath for the drum, the skin keeping time. If there's no recording near you, pluck something: a rubber band, a taut thread. Listen to how long the sound lasts before it's gone. If you pray, you can let Waheguru sound inside, as quietly as the end of a plucked note. The bell holds the time.

Tanti saaj. String instruments: the rabab, the saranda, the taus, the dilruba, the older voices of kirtan, with the pakhawaj drum beneath them. Today's word. Your week: the hard century, kingdom and loss, renewal and today, year three close, raag, ghar, and tanti saaj.
Your line: strings and skin. Today, in whatever music finds you, listen for one string and one drum, and notice which one you follow. Day one thousand sixty-four.

howItsDone: Kirtan in gurdwaras today is heard with harmonium and tabla, and some ragis and kirtan schools also teach and perform on the older string instruments, the rabab, saranda, taus and dilruba, with the pakhawaj drum.

original.note: Gurmukhi: string instruments, the family of the rabab, saranda, taus and dilruba in the older kirtan.

trapdoor: what you thought: kirtan means a harmonium and a tabla.
what it means: the older kirtan was carried by strings, tanti saaj, with the pakhawaj drum beneath them.

what a scholar hears: tradition ties the rabab to Bhai Mardana in the janamsakhis; bowed strings like the saranda, taus and dilruba can hold and slide between notes, which suits raga-based kirtan, and some musicians work to restore them beside the harmonium.
recall: the four sons of Guru Gobind Singh

notes: Descriptions of instruments (rabab with a skin-covered wooden body; saranda bowed; taus carved like a peacock; dilruba a lighter cousin of the taus; pakhawaj a barrel drum played on both ends) are general organology; please confirm.
The teach avoids crediting particular Gurus with introducing the saranda, taus or dilruba, since those attributions are traditional and vary; a Keeper may wish to add them as 'tradition says'.
'Some musicians and teachers have worked to bring the older strings back' refers to the gurmat sangeet revival; kept general on purpose.
Japji pauri 27 paraphrased (countless instruments and players at the Creator's gate); confirm.
Day 1064 is a week end; the week looked back on runs from day 1058 to 1064, across the year boundary.
Editor: softened 'they carry kirtan every day' (sweeping claim).
